title: Typed With Sticky Keys
statement:
Someone meant to type the word intended, but their keyboard is sticky: when they press a key, that character may come out one or more times instead of exactly once. Keys never come out zero times, and no stray characters appear.

You get the text that actually came out, typed. Return true if typed could be the result of typing intended on this keyboard, and false otherwise.

examples.why: The runs are m, oo, n in the word and mm, oooo, nn in the text. Every run kept its letter and only grew.
The word needs two o's in a row. A sticky key can add letters, never remove them.
The extra cc is fine, but the space and the d at the end were never part of the word. Stopping once the word is used up would miss them.

constraints: Both strings hold printable ASCII characters
hints: Walk through both strings at the same time. When does the typed character match what you expect, and when is it a harmless repeat?
Keep pointer i in intended and j in typed. If the characters match, advance both. If not, typed[j] is only allowed when it equals typed[j − 1], the key that just stuck.
When typed runs out, every character of intended must have been used. Do not stop as soon as intended is used up: the rest of typed must still be repeats of its last character.

explain.intuition:
Think of both strings as runs of the same character: "moon" is m·oo·n. The sticky keyboard can only make each run longer. So the texts match when they have the same run letters in the same order and every typed run is at least as long as the word's run.

Two pointers check this without building the runs. Move through typed one character at a time. If it matches the next expected character of the word, consume both. If it does not, the only excuse is that it repeats the character just typed. Anything else is a stray key, and the answer is no.
steps: Set i = 0 in intended. Loop j over every index of typed.
Else if j > 0 and typed[j] === typed[j − 1], it is a sticky repeat; skip it.
pitfalls: Returning true as soon as the word is used up. Leftover characters in typed must still be repeats, as in "abcc d".
Checking for a repeat before checking for a match. With intended = "aab" and typed = "aab", the second a is a real letter of the word, but the repeat check would swallow it.
Forgetting to check that the whole word was used. "aaa" against "aa" ends with one letter unmatched.

solutions.title: Compare runs
solutions.idea: Split both strings into (character, length) runs. They must have the same characters in order, and each typed run must be at least as long.

solutions.title: Two pointers
solutions.idea: Consume a word character on a match; otherwise allow the typed character only if it repeats the previous typed character.

followups: Keys may also be dropped once in a while (at most one missing character). How does the check change?
You must test one typed string against a dictionary of 100 000 words. What would you precompute?
